title: Backpropagation by hand and in NumPy
summary: Computational graphs, the backward pass as repeated chain rule, vanishing and exploding gradients, and a complete neural network trained from scratch in NumPy with gradient checking.
syllabus: NOAI Mathematics: chain rule, computational graphs and automatic differentiation

lessons.title: Computational graphs
lessons.summary: Breaking any calculation into small nodes so that values flow forward and gradients flow backward.
objectives: You can draw a computational graph for a small expression
You can compute the forward values
You can write each node's local derivative

concepts.name: Calculations as graphs
concepts.explain: Any formula, like L = (wx + b − y)², can be drawn as a graph of simple operations (multiply, add, subtract, square). The forward pass evaluates nodes left to right; each node also knows its local derivative with respect to its inputs.
concepts.analogy: A recipe written as a flowchart: chop, then fry, then mix; each step only needs to know about its own inputs.

visual.shows: A node-and-edge graph of the expression with values filling in as the forward pass proceeds.
visual.interaction: Edit inputs w, x, b, y; choose expressions from a menu; step the forward pass.
visual.aha: Big formulas are just chains of tiny operations, each easy to differentiate.

concepts.name: Local gradient rules
concepts.explain: Each operation has a simple local rule: an add node passes the gradient unchanged to both inputs; a multiply node sends each input the gradient times the other input; a square node multiplies by 2 × its input. Backprop only ever uses these local rules.
concepts.analogy: Each station on a relay only needs to know how to pass the baton to the next runner.

visual.shows: Cards for add, multiply, max, square and sigmoid gates showing an upstream gradient arriving and how it is split to the inputs.
visual.interaction: Edit the inputs and upstream gradient on each card; the outgoing gradients update.
visual.aha: 'Add distributes, multiply swaps, max routes': three patterns cover most of backprop.

lessons.title: Backprop step by step
lessons.summary: Running the backward pass through a small network, multiplying local gradients, and summing where paths branch.
objectives: You can compute gradients for a two-layer network by hand
You can explain why gradients add where a value is used twice
You can relate backprop to the chain rule

concepts.name: The backward pass
concepts.explain: Starting from dL/dL = 1 at the loss, move backwards through the graph: at each node multiply the incoming (upstream) gradient by the local derivative and pass it to the node's inputs. When a value feeds several nodes, its gradients from each path are added.
concepts.analogy: Tracing blame for a late project backwards: each person's share is their manager's share times how much they contributed.

visual.shows: A graph for a single neuron with squared loss; after the forward pass, each backward step lights one edge and shows 'upstream × local = gradient', ending with ∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂b.
visual.interaction: Step forward and backward; edit values; switch to a graph where x is used twice to see gradients sum.
visual.aha: Backprop is the chain rule applied mechanically, one edge at a time.

concepts.name: Gradients through a network
concepts.explain: In an MLP, the gradient for a weight equals the upstream gradient at its output neuron times the activation feeding into it. Gradients flowing back through a layer are multiplied by the transposed weight matrix and the activation's derivative.
concepts.analogy: Water flowing back through a pipe network: the amount through each pipe depends on its width (weight) and on the valve (activation derivative).

visual.shows: A NeuralNet diagram of a 2-3-2 network where, after a forward pass, a backward wave colours each weight by gradient magnitude and sign.
visual.interaction: Play the backward wave; change the target output; switch activations to see where gradients shrink.
visual.aha: Weights connected to strongly active inputs and large errors get the biggest updates.

lessons.title: Vanishing and exploding gradients
lessons.summary: Why gradients shrink or blow up in deep networks and the fixes: ReLU, good initialisation, normalisation, residual connections and clipping.
objectives: You can explain vanishing gradients as a product of small factors
You can explain exploding gradients and NaN losses
You can match fixes (ReLU, He init, BatchNorm, residuals, clipping) to problems

concepts.name: Gradient size by layer
concepts.explain: The gradient at an early layer is a product of one factor per later layer (weights times activation derivatives). With sigmoid (derivative at most 0.25) or small weights, it shrinks exponentially with depth; with large weights it grows exponentially. Early layers then learn far too slowly or training blows up.
concepts.analogy: A whisper passed down a 20-person line fades to nothing; a shout amplified by each person becomes deafening.

visual.shows: Bars for gradient norm at each of up to 30 layers on a log scale, recomputed for a randomly initialised deep network.
visual.interaction: Choose the activation, the weight-initialisation scale and the depth; toggle residual connections and BatchNorm.
visual.aha: Gradient health depends on activation, initialisation and architecture together, and each fix targets one cause.

concepts.name: Residual connections as a highway
concepts.explain: A residual connection adds a layer's input to its output: y = x + F(x). In the backward pass the '+ x' path passes gradient straight through unchanged, so even very deep networks keep a strong signal to early layers. This is the key idea of ResNet.
concepts.analogy: An expressway that bypasses all the traffic lights: even if local roads are jammed, traffic still gets through.

visual.shows: A stack of 20 blocks with and without skip arrows; a pulse of gradient travels backward and its brightness fades in the plain stack but not in the residual stack.
visual.interaction: Toggle skips; change depth; play the pulse.
visual.aha: The identity path keeps gradients alive, which is why residual networks can be hundreds of layers deep.

checkpoint_focus: Residual connections give a gradient highway

lessons.title: A neural network from scratch in NumPy
lessons.summary: Implementing the forward pass, loss, backward pass and update for a small classifier, and verifying gradients numerically.
objectives: You can implement forward and backward passes for a one-hidden-layer network in NumPy
You can write a training loop that reduces loss
You can check analytic gradients with finite differences

concepts.name: The training cycle
concepts.explain: Every training step does four things: forward pass (predictions), loss, backward pass (gradients), update (gradient descent). For softmax with cross-entropy the gradient at the logits is simply p − y, which makes the backward pass compact.
concepts.analogy: The cycle of a CCA training session: perform, get scored, review what went wrong, adjust, repeat.

visual.shows: A circular four-stage diagram linked to the code lines for each stage and a decision boundary on a 2D dataset that improves with each loop.
visual.interaction: Play or step loops; pause on a stage to see the corresponding NumPy code and array shapes.
visual.aha: All of deep learning training is this four-step loop, repeated.

concepts.name: The backward pass in matrix form
concepts.explain: For a batch X of shape (N, D): Z1 = X W1 + b1, A1 = ReLU(Z1), Z2 = A1 W2 + b2, P = softmax(Z2). Going backwards: dZ2 = (P − Y)/N; dW2 = A1ᵀ dZ2; db2 = dZ2.sum(axis=0); dA1 = dZ2 W2ᵀ; dZ1 = dA1 * (Z1 > 0); dW1 = Xᵀ dZ1; db1 = dZ1.sum(axis=0). Two rules write most of it for you: every gradient has the same shape as the thing it is the gradient of, and a weight gradient is (layer input)ᵀ times (upstream gradient), with biases summed over the batch.
concepts.analogy: Packing for a return trip: every item you brought out (each forward array) comes back in the same suitcase slot (same shape) on the way home.

visual.shows: The seven backward lines for a network with N = 4 examples, D = 3 features, H = 5 hidden units and K = 2 classes, each with its shape annotation (for example dW1 = X.T @ dZ1: (3, 4) @ (4, 5) → (3, 5)) and a small heat map of the resulting array.
visual.interaction: Step line by line; change N, D, H or K and watch every shape update; inject a bug (drop a transpose, forget the ReLU mask, forget the /N) and see which shape check or gradient check fails.
visual.aha: Matching each gradient's shape to its parameter's shape writes most of the backward pass for you.

concepts.name: Gradient checking
concepts.explain: To test your backward pass, nudge one weight by a tiny ε, recompute the loss, and estimate the derivative as (L(w + ε) − L(w − ε))/(2ε). It should closely match your analytic gradient; a big mismatch means a bug. Use the central difference with ε around 1e-5 in float64: a larger ε adds truncation error from curvature, and a smaller one adds rounding error from subtracting nearly equal numbers. PyTorch's torch.autograd.gradcheck does exactly this.
concepts.analogy: Checking your mental sum with a quick estimate: if they disagree wildly, something is off.

visual.shows: For each parameter, the analytic gradient, the numerical estimate and their relative error on a log scale, with a pass/fail threshold.
visual.interaction: Slide ε from 1e-1 to 1e-10 to see error fall then rise again (floating-point round-off); inject a bug into the backward code to see checks fail.
visual.aha: Numerical gradients are slow but reliable referees for your hand-written backprop.

checkpoint_focus: Shapes of W, b and activations in a batch
dW = inputᵀ @ upstream; db = upstream.sum(axis=0); ReLU mask (Z1 > 0)
